idiom_name: #private-field composition + using/Symbol.dispose with the Disposable types
implementation_notes: TypeScript keeps the JavaScript story and adds types: the whole is a class whose parts live in #private fields or private readonly properties, the interface it presents is an interface/type it implements (so no part type needs to be exported), and lifecycle uses the disposable protocol - TypeScript 5.2 added using/await using declarations, the Disposable/AsyncDisposable types, DisposableStack/AsyncDisposableStack and SuppressedError - so a whole that owns resources implements [Symbol.dispose] and callers scope it. readonly prevents reassigning a part reference but not mutating the part, and structural typing means any object with a matching shape satisfies the whole's type unless the constructor is private; ownership therefore remains encapsulation plus convention, not a type-level guarantee.
pitfalls: Structural typing lets an object literal stand in for the whole wherever the type is structural; keep real wholes behind private constructors and factories so a shape-compatible object cannot bypass ownership.
Nothing forces the caller to bind the whole with `using`: disposal is opt-in per declaration, and a leaked whole keeps file handles and listeners alive until the process ends.
`readonly` on a part field is not immutability of the part: a getter that returns the internal array (or the part objects) still lets callers mutate state behind the whole.
